notes:
I've now gathered substantial material. Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Ezra 2:1-23, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## Ezra 2:1-23 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is a register of the first wave of returning exiles under Zerubbabel (538 BC). The list is nearly identical to Nehemiah 7:6–69. It names leaders first, then families by patriarchal descent (vv. 3–20), then by ancestral towns (vv. 21–35), then priests, Levites, and temple servants (vv. 36–58), then those with uncertain genealogies (vv. 59–63), a grand total, and freewill offerings (vv. 64–69).

---

### v. 1 — "Now these are the people of the province who came up from the captivity…"

**"The province"** means Judea, now reduced from an independent kingdom to a mere province of the Persian Empire (Pulpit Commentary; JFB; Gill). The phrase is used in contrast to Babylon, the imperial capital, and signals Ezra's "foreign standpoint" as a writer in Persia (Pulpit). Ellicott adds that the returnees came from "the captivity" — which had itself become almost a generic name — and became "children of the province," i.e., the Judaean province of Persia.

**"Every one unto his city"** indicates that returnees settled not only in Jerusalem but also in outlying towns such as Jericho, Tekoa, Gibeon, Mizpah, and Zanoah (Pulpit; JFB). JFB explains this refers either to the city occupied by ancestors or, since much land was desolate, to the city "rebuilt and allotted to him now."

- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)
- [JFB via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/ezra-2.html)
- [Gill's Exposition](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/2.htm)
- [Ellicott's Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 2 — "accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah…"

**Eleven names appear**, but the parallel in Nehemiah 7:7 lists twelve (adding Nahamani). Most commentators consider the set of twelve deliberate, representing the twelve tribes, and that one name accidentally dropped from the Ezra text during copying (Pulpit; EnduringWord/Kidner; Ellicott). Kidner writes: "The choice of twelve, like that of the twelve apostles, was a tacit declaration that the community they led was no mere rump or fragment but the embodiment of the people of Israel."

**Zerubbabel**: Appointed Persian governor over Judah, and a lineal descendant of the royal house of David — "the heir to the throne of David" (EnduringWord/Adeney). He is probably the same person called Sheshbazzar in Ezra 1:8, since both are credited with laying the temple foundation (Ezra 3:8; 5:16) (EnduringWord). The Pulpit Commentary notes that his Persian title "Tirshatha" (v. 63) means "the Feared," an old Persian term for governor.

**Jeshua**: The high priest (also called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah), son of Josedech, Zerubbabel's fellow-leader (Gill; EnduringWord/Kidner).

**Nehemiah and Mordecai**: Not the famous Nehemiah who rebuilt the walls, nor Esther's kinsman Mordecai — others of the same name (Geneva Study Bible; Gill; EnduringWord/Trapp). Gill notes that John Lightfoot thought this Nehemiah was the same as the book's Nehemiah, but this is widely disputed since Nehemiah the wall-builder came to Jerusalem in the 20th year of Artaxerxes, decades later.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)
- [Geneva Study Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/ezra-2.html)
- [Gill's Exposition](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "the descendants of Parosh, 2,172"

The family names that follow (vv. 3–20) are patriarchal — the list names the heads of families, not individuals, so the total number of people was substantially larger since women and children are not counted (EnduringWord). The name **Parosh** means "flea" (EnduringWord/Guzik). Nothing more is known of him (Gill).

Concerning numerical discrepancies with Nehemiah 7: of the 42 numbers in Ezra 2:3–60, eighteen differ from the Nehemiah parallel, mostly by small margins — evidence of the "corruption to which numbers are liable from the mistakes of copyists" (Pulpit).

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "the descendants of Shephatiah, 372"

**Shephatiah** means "Yahweh has judged" (EnduringWord). The number 372 is the same in both Ezra and Nehemiah for this family. Gill notes that beyond the numbers, no further details about this family are known.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Gill's Exposition](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "the descendants of Arah, 775"

**Arah** means "wild ox" (EnduringWord). Here the Ezra count (775) differs significantly from Nehemiah 7:10, which gives only 652. Matthew Poole (cited by EnduringWord and JFB) offers the traditional explanation: 775 gave their names at the initial muster in Babylon, but some died, "others changed their minds, others were hindered by sickness, or other casualties… so there came only six hundred and fifty-two to Jerusalem." This principle is applied to all similar numerical differences.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [JFB via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/ezra-2.html)

---

### v. 6 — "the descendants of Pahath-moab (through the line of Jeshua and Joab), 2,812"

**Pahath-moab** is the largest family group in the list. The dual descent "through the line of Jeshua and Joab" suggests this clan traced its lineage through two notable ancestors. The family number 2,812 in Ezra is confirmed by 1 Esdras against Nehemiah's 2,818 (Ellicott).

- [Ellicott's Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/2.htm)
- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 7 — "the descendants of Elam, 1,254"

**Elam** — not the region but a personal name. A second "other Elam" appears at v. 31 with exactly the same number (1,254), suggesting two distinct families sharing the name (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes no special significance beyond the record.

---

### vv. 8–12 — Zattu (945), Zaccai (760), Bani (642), Bebai (623), Azgad (1,222)

EnduringWord provides the meanings of several names:
- **Zaccai**: either "pure" or a shortened form of Zechariah
- **Bani**: shortened form of Benaiah, "Yahweh has built"
- **Bebai**: "pupil of the eye"
- **Azgad**: "Gad is strong"

Ellicott notes that for Bani (v. 10), 1 Esdras agrees with Nehemiah in giving 648 rather than 642. For Bebai (v. 11), Ezra's 623 stands against Nehemiah's 628.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Ellicott's Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 13 — "the descendants of Adonikam, 666"

**Adonikam** means "my Lord has arisen" (EnduringWord). The number **666** is noticed by some readers for its later significance in Revelation 13:18, but none of the traditional commentators I found draw a connection — it is simply a census figure here. Ellicott notes that Nehemiah and 1 Esdras both correct 666 to 667, a small scribal difference.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Ellicott's Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 14 — "the descendants of Bigvai, 2,056"

The second-largest family group after Pahath-moab. Nothing more is known of Bigvai (Gill).

---

### v. 15 — "the descendants of Adin, 454"

**Adin** means "voluptuous" or "dainty" (EnduringWord). Ellicott notes Ezra's 454 here stands against Nehemiah's 655.

---

### v. 16 — "the descendants of Ater (through Hezekiah), 98"

**Ater** means "lefty" (EnduringWord). The specification "through Hezekiah" may indicate descent from King Hezekiah, or from another notable Hezekiah. The Geneva Study Bible says: "Who were of the posterity of Hezekiah." At only 98, this is the smallest family group in the list of families (not counting towns). Gill notes nothing further.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)
- [Geneva Study Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/ezra-2.html)

---

### v. 17 — "the descendants of Bezai, 323"

**Bezai** is likely a shortened form of Bezaleel, meaning "in the shadow of God" (EnduringWord). Ellicott notes Ezra's 323 stands against Nehemiah's 324.

---

### v. 18 — "the descendants of Jorah, 112"

**Jorah** means "autumn rain" (EnduringWord). In Nehemiah 7:24 the name appears as "Hariph." A small family of 112.

---

### v. 19 — "the descendants of Hashum, 223"

**Hashum** means "broad nose" (EnduringWord). One of several families whose names reflect physical characteristics or perhaps nicknames.

---

### v. 20 — "the descendants of Gibbar, 95"

This verse marks an important transition. The Pulpit Commentary says: for **"Gibbar"** we should probably read **"Gibeon"** (as in Nehemiah 7:25). The writer here "passes from persons to places, making the latter portion of his list topographical." Ellicott agrees: "Nehemiah substitutes Gibeon for Gibbar." Gibeon was a well-known town in Benjamin (Joshua 18:25).

From this point through v. 35, returnees are identified by their ancestral towns rather than patriarchal family names.

- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)
- [Ellicott's Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 21 — "the men of Bethlehem, 123"

The Geneva Study Bible notes that "children" when joined with place names (as here: "men of") means "inhabitants" — i.e., those whose ancestral homes were in these locations. Bethlehem, the city of David, sent only 123. The small number reflects how thoroughly the land had been depopulated.

- [Geneva Study Bible](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/ezra-2.html)
- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)

---

### v. 22 — "the men of Netophah, 56"

Netophah was a small town near Bethlehem (Kretzmann). Just 56 returnees claimed it as their ancestral home. Kretzmann notes: "a small town near Bethlehem."

- [Kretzmann's Popular Commentary via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezra-2.html)

---

### v. 23 — "the men of Anathoth, 128"

JFB offers the richest comment on this verse:

> "It is pleasant to see so many of this Jewish town returning. It was a city of the Levites; but the people spurned Jeremiah's warning and called forth against themselves one of his severest predictions (Jeremiah 32:27-35). This prophecy was fulfilled in the Assyrian conquest. Anathoth was laid waste and continued a heap of ruins. But the people, having been brought during the captivity to a better state of mind, returned, and their city was rebuilt."

Kretzmann similarly notes: "a Levitical city, the home of Jeremiah, against which he had prophesied in one of his severest predictions."

The Precept Austin commentary connects this to Jeremiah 32:6-15, where God told Jeremiah to redeem family property in Anathoth as a sign that "houses and fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land." The 128 returnees from Anathoth represent the literal fulfillment of that prophetic sign.

- [JFB via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/ezra-2.html)
- [Kretzmann's Popular Commentary via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezra-2.html)
- [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary)

---

## Denominational and Tradition-Specific Observations

Because Ezra 2 is a genealogical register, the major Protestant traditions do not significantly diverge on its interpretation. All treat it as a historically reliable record. However, several distinct emphases emerged:

**Reformed / Presbyterian (Kidner, Adeney — cited by EnduringWord):** Stress God's sovereign faithfulness in preserving families and bringing a remnant home. Kidner calls the chapter "a monument to God's care" and notes that relating people "to those local and family circles which humanise a society and orientate an individual… is God's way, who 'setteth the solitary in families' (Psalm 68:6)." The twelve leaders represent the twelve tribes, signalling continuity of the covenant people, not a mere fragment.

- [EnduringWord citing Kidner and Adeney](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)

**Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Gill emphasizes that only the tribes of Judah and Benjamin are principally in view, though some from other tribes also returned. Garner-Howes draws three practical lessons: "(1) The Lord preserved the Jews by their distinctive families in the captivity; (2) the Lord always has those of His special ministers to lead in His worship; (3) one must possess the right qualifications to be a part of God's people (Matthew 7:21-23); (4) those willing to suffer hardship in the Lord's cause are a small minority."

- [Gill's Exposition](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/2.htm)
- [Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezra-2.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (EnduringWord / David Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes application — that the list reveals real people with genuine human flavour (names meaning flea, broad nose, lefty), and that God knows His people individually. He also draws a parallel to modern Jewish emigration from Iraq to Israel, citing David Ben-Gurion.

- [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-2/)

**Brethren (Grant's Commentary):** Grant sees typological significance: "Babylon means 'confusion,' so that Judah is pictured as being captives to a state of confusion, as is repeated in the history of the professing church." The Urim and Thummim, absent at the return, point to Christ: "He is the High Priest who has the Urim and Thummim."

- [Grant's Commentary via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/ezra-2.html)

**Lutheran (Kretzmann):** Treats the list straightforwardly as historical record, noting that the 12 priestly heads who led the return "represented, in a way, the twelve tribes of Israel." No distinctive Lutheran doctrinal emphasis separates this reading from others.

- [Kretzmann's Popular Commentary via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezra-2.html)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Constable's Expository Notes):** Constable notes that the designations "sons of" and "men of" represent the two ways exiles proved Jewish ancestry: by family genealogy or by residence in Palestine. "Few of the returning exiles had personally lived in the Promised Land, but many could give evidence that their ancestors had lived in a particular town and or had owned property there." He treats the numerical discrepancies as arising from the use of different source documents and scribal error.

- [Dr. Constable's Expository Notes via StudyLight](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-2.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** I was unable to search these sources before hitting my search limit. The Catholic commentaries at newadvent.org and the Orthodox resources at oca.org would likely treat Ezra 2 as part of the canonical historical books, read liturgically and affirming the continuity of God's people. The Vulgate (Latin) tradition has some variant readings, such as 40,000 drachmas of gold in v. 69 (noted by Gill).

**On the numerical discrepancies:** The sum of individual items in Ezra adds to 29,818, but v. 64 gives the total as 42,360. Gill says the Jewish chronology Seder Olam Rabbah explains the missing 12,000+ as members of other tribes not individually itemized. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott lean toward scribal corruption in the original documents. Constable notes some suggest women and children account for the difference, but "this would be a small number for 30,000 men."

- [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/2.htm)
- [Gill's Exposition](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/2.htm)
- [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-2-commentary)

---

*Note: I was unable to search for Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) readings, or for modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) due to search limits, so those perspectives are absent above. What is presented comes from the Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal/Charismatic, Brethren, and Lutheran commentators I was able to access.*
